fathers/origen/roles/0: Catechist and head of the Alexandrian school
fathers/origen/summary: Origen Adamantius (c. 185–c. 254), the most prolific and influential theologian of the pre-Nicene church, produced the Hexapla, the first systematic theology (On First Principles) and commentaries on almost the entire Bible, giving Christianity its method of spiritual exegesis — while some of his speculations were posthumously condemned.
fathers/origen/story:
Origen was born in Alexandria around 185 to Christian parents. When his father Leonides was martyred in 202, the teenage Origen reportedly wished to follow him and was prevented only by his mother hiding his clothes (Eusebius, Church History 6.2). Bishop Demetrius soon entrusted him with catechetical instruction, and he lived an intensely ascetic life; Eusebius’ report that he castrated himself in literal obedience to Matthew 19:12 is accepted by many historians but doubted by others.

He studied philosophy, probably under Ammonius Saccas, the teacher of Plotinus, and learned Hebrew in order to compare texts. In Alexandria he began the Hexapla, a six-column synopsis of the Hebrew Old Testament, its Greek transliteration and four Greek versions, a landmark of ancient textual scholarship. With the patronage of Ambrose, a wealthy convert, he dictated to teams of stenographers, producing commentaries, homilies and treatises; Jerome later credited him with some 2,000 works.

Around 220–230 he wrote On First Principles (Peri Archon), the first attempt at a systematic Christian theology. It begins with the ‘rule of faith’ handed down by the apostles and then explores open questions: the eternal generation of the Son, the pre-existence and fall of rational souls, the freedom of the will, and the hope that God will ultimately restore all things (apokatastasis). His ordination as presbyter in Caesarea around 230, without Demetrius’ consent, led to a break with Alexandria. He settled in Caesarea Maritima, where he founded a school and library whose curriculum, described by his pupil Gregory Thaumaturgus, led students through logic, natural science, ethics and theology to scripture.

In Caesarea he preached through the Bible, wrote Against Celsus (c. 248), the most substantial early reply to a pagan critic, and On Prayer and the Exhortation to Martyrdom. Under the Decian persecution (250) he was imprisoned and tortured; he died some time later, probably in Tyre around 253–254.

Origen’s reputation became a battleground. Defended by Pamphilus and Eusebius and mined by the Cappadocians, his ideas — especially as systematised by later monks — were attacked by Methodius, Epiphanius and Jerome in the Origenist controversy of the 390s, and fifteen anathemas against ‘Origenist’ teachings (pre-existence of souls, apokatastasis) were issued under Justinian in 543 and associated with the Second Council of Constantinople (553). Whether they accurately describe Origen himself is still debated. Most of his Greek works were lost; much survives only in the Latin translations of Rufinus and Jerome.
fathers/origen/roots/0/text: Origen learned Hebrew, compiled the Hexapla and consulted Jewish scholars in Caesarea, making scripture the centre of all his work.
fathers/origen/roots/1/text: He inherited from Philo, via Clement, the allegorical method and the threefold sense of scripture (body, soul, spirit) set out in On First Principles book 4.
fathers/origen/roots/2/text: His theology of a transcendent Father, eternal intelligible realm, pre-existent minds and the soul’s ascent reflects Middle Platonism and the teaching of Ammonius Saccas.
fathers/origen/roots/3/text: On First Principles opens with the ‘rule of faith’ preached by the apostles as the fixed point for all speculation.
fathers/origen/roots/4/text: Much of his thought on free will and the goodness of the one Creator is directed against Valentinian determinism and Marcion’s separation of the two Testaments.
fathers/origen/roots/5/text: He developed the Logos theology of Justin and the Alexandrian synthesis of Clement.
fathers/origen/keyTeachings/0: Scripture has literal, moral and spiritual senses; the spiritual sense reveals Christ throughout the Old Testament
fathers/origen/keyTeachings/1: The Son is eternally generated by the Father (‘there was no when he was not’), yet subordinate as image of the Father
fathers/origen/keyTeachings/2: Rational beings are free; evil arises from the misuse of freedom, not from matter or fate
fathers/origen/keyTeachings/3: God’s punishments are remedial, opening the hope of the restoration of all (apokatastasis)
fathers/origen/keyTeachings/4: The Christian life is an ascent of the soul through purification and contemplation to union with the Word
fathers/origen/keyTeachings/5: The Song of Songs as the love of the soul and the church for Christ
fathers/origen/works/0/note: First systematic theology; survives mostly in Rufinus’ softened Latin version.
fathers/origen/works/1/note: Eight-book reply to the Platonist Celsus’ True Word (c. 178).
fathers/origen/works/2/note: Six-column edition of the Old Testament; used by Eusebius and Jerome at Caesarea.
fathers/origen/works/3/note: Extensive exegesis, partly directed against the Valentinian Heracleon.
fathers/origen/works/4/title: Homilies and Commentary on the Song of Songs
fathers/origen/works/4/note: Founded the mystical interpretation of the Song.
fathers/origen/works/5/title: On Prayer and Exhortation to Martyrdom
fathers/origen/works/5/note: The earliest Christian treatise on prayer, including a commentary on the Lord’s Prayer.
fathers/origen/doctrineContributions/0/t: Introduced eternal generation and the language of three hypostases, giving the vocabulary used by both sides in the Arian controversy.
fathers/origen/doctrineContributions/1/t: Founded scientific biblical scholarship and the classic theory of the spiritual sense.
fathers/origen/doctrineContributions/2/t: Proposed remedial punishment and universal restoration, a hope later shared by Gregory of Nyssa but condemned in its ‘Origenist’ form in 543/553.
fathers/origen/doctrineContributions/3/t: His model of spiritual ascent and his reading of the Song of Songs shaped all later Christian mysticism.
fathers/origen/doctrineContributions/4/t: Strong defence of free will against astrological and Gnostic determinism.
fathers/origen/laterInfluence/0/text: Basil and Gregory of Nazianzus compiled an anthology of his writings, the Philokalia of Origen; Gregory of Nyssa adopted much of his eschatology and mysticism.
fathers/origen/laterInfluence/1/text: Through Evagrius Ponticus and John Cassian, Origen’s spirituality shaped Eastern and Western monastic theology.
fathers/origen/laterInfluence/2/text: Ambrose, Jerome and, indirectly, the medieval Latin fourfold sense of scripture depend on him.
fathers/origen/laterInfluence/3/text: Erasmus admired him above Augustine; Luther disliked his allegory and is reported to have said that ‘in all of Origen there is not one word about Christ’.
fathers/origen/laterInfluence/4/text: The 20th-century ressourcement (de Lubac, Daniélou, von Balthasar) rehabilitated him; universalists from Moltmann to David Bentley Hart claim his heritage.
fathers/origen/reception/0/text: Not a saint; honoured as a great teacher and exegete (Benedict XVI devoted two catecheses to him in 2007), while some propositions attributed to him remain condemned.
fathers/origen/reception/1/text: Named among heretics in the anathemas associated with the Fifth Ecumenical Council (553); his exegesis and spirituality nevertheless pervade Orthodox tradition.
fathers/origen/reception/2/text: Respected as part of the Alexandrian heritage, but treated cautiously because of the later condemnations.
fathers/origen/reception/3/text: Valued as a biblical scholar and textual critic; his allegory and speculative theology have been criticised since the Reformation.
fathers/origen/controversies/0: Ordination at Caesarea and break with Bishop Demetrius of Alexandria (c. 230–231)
fathers/origen/controversies/1: Pre-existence of souls and the restoration of all things (apokatastasis)
fathers/origen/controversies/2: Subordinationist elements in his Trinitarian theology
fathers/origen/controversies/3: The Origenist controversies of the 390s (Epiphanius, Jerome, Theophilus) and the 6th century
fathers/origen/controversies/4: Condemnation under Justinian (543) and association with the Council of Constantinople II (553)
fathers/origen/quote/text: The Scriptures were written by the Spirit of God and have a meaning not only such as is apparent at first sight, but also another which escapes the notice of most.
fathers/athenagoras/roles/1: Apologist to Marcus Aurelius and Commodus
fathers/athenagoras/summary: A Christian philosopher of Athens who c. 177 addressed to Marcus Aurelius and Commodus the Embassy (Plea) for the Christians, the most polished of the second-century apologies. He answered charges of atheism, cannibalism and incest, and gave a notably balanced early account of Father, Son and Spirit as united in power and distinct in order.
fathers/athenagoras/story:
Almost nothing is known of Athenagoras beyond his writings. The tenth-century manuscript (Arethas codex, Paris. gr. 451) calls him 'Athenagoras the Athenian, a Christian philosopher'. A late report by Philip of Side (fifth century) that he headed the catechetical school of Alexandria and taught Clement is not trusted by historians. Methodius of Olympus quotes him c. 300, but otherwise he was little cited in antiquity.

The Embassy (Presbeia, usually called the Plea or Legatio) is addressed to 'the emperors Marcus Aurelius Antoninus and Lucius Aurelius Commodus, conquerors of Armenia and Sarmatia, and above all philosophers', which dates it to 176–180, most likely 177, the year of the persecution at Lyon. Written in elegant Attic Greek, it adopts the form of a petition and argues that Christians, alone among the empire's peoples, are punished for a name rather than for crimes.

Athenagoras answers three charges: atheism, 'Thyestean banquets' (cannibalism) and 'Oedipal intercourse' (incest). Against atheism he quotes poets and philosophers from Euripides to Plato's Timaeus to show that the best pagans also affirmed one God, and he explains that Christians worship 'one God, uncreated, eternal, invisible', with his Son, who is the Father's Word, Mind and Wisdom, and the Holy Spirit, 'an effluence of God, flowing from him and returning like a ray of the sun'. He insists on 'their power in union and their distinction in order' (Leg. 10, 12). Against cannibalism he notes that Christians condemn even watching gladiatorial killings and regard women who use drugs to procure abortion as murderers (Leg. 35). Against immorality he describes Christian chastity, permitting marriage only for children and calling second marriage 'decent adultery' (Leg. 33).

A treatise On the Resurrection of the Dead, transmitted under his name, argues philosophically that God is able and willing to raise bodies and that human nature, being a unity of soul and body, requires it. Its authenticity is disputed: R. M. Grant and others assigned it to a later author, while Bernard Pouderon and others defend Athenagoras's authorship.

Athenagoras was never the object of a significant cult and does not figure prominently in liturgical calendars. Modern scholarship values him as the most philosophically careful of the Greek apologists, an important witness to pre-Nicene Trinitarian thinking and to early Christian moral teaching on abortion, infanticide and the games.
fathers/athenagoras/roots/0/text: He presents God as uncreated, impassible and grasped by mind and reason, and quotes Plato's Timaeus on the maker and father of the universe.
fathers/athenagoras/roots/1/text: He uses Stoic terms of providence and divine reason (logos) pervading the world, while rejecting Stoic materialism.
fathers/athenagoras/roots/2/text: His Plea is a carefully constructed forensic speech in Attic Greek, following classical petition form.
fathers/athenagoras/roots/3/text: He develops the apologetic arguments and Logos theology of Justin Martyr.
fathers/athenagoras/roots/4/text: He appeals to the prophets Moses, Isaiah and Jeremiah as inspired by the Spirit like a flautist playing a flute (Leg. 9).
fathers/athenagoras/keyTeachings/0: Christians are not atheists: they worship one God together with his Son and Spirit
fathers/athenagoras/keyTeachings/1: Son and Spirit united in power and distinguished in order
fathers/athenagoras/keyTeachings/2: The Son as the Father's eternal Word and Mind, not created
fathers/athenagoras/keyTeachings/3: Christian morality: rejection of abortion, infanticide and the gladiatorial games
fathers/athenagoras/keyTeachings/4: Resurrection of the body as required by the unity of human nature (if On the Resurrection is his)
fathers/athenagoras/works/0/note: Apology addressed to Marcus Aurelius and Commodus answering charges of atheism, cannibalism and incest.
fathers/athenagoras/works/1/title: On the Resurrection of the Dead
fathers/athenagoras/works/1/note: Philosophical treatise on bodily resurrection; authorship disputed.
fathers/athenagoras/doctrineContribution: Among the clearest pre-Nicene statements of unity and distinction in God: Father, Son and Spirit one in power, distinct in order.
Developed the argument that the best philosophers glimpsed the one God, so Christian monotheism is rational.
Witness to early Christian rejection of abortion and exposure of infants, and to a strict ethic of marriage.
fathers/athenagoras/laterInfluence/0/tex: Quoted by Methodius of Olympus; otherwise little used, but his arguments were absorbed into the common apologetic tradition.
fathers/athenagoras/laterInfluence/1/tex: His works survived through Arethas of Caesarea's collection of apologists (914).
fathers/athenagoras/laterInfluence/2/tex: Studied as a key source for pre-Nicene Trinitarian theology and early Christian ethics; often cited in modern debates on abortion.
fathers/athenagoras/reception/0/text: Honoured as an apologist and ancient ecclesiastical writer; not widely venerated liturgically.
fathers/athenagoras/reception/1/text: Respected as an early Christian philosopher of Athens; his name was later borne by Ecumenical Patriarch Athenagoras I.
fathers/athenagoras/reception/2/text: Valued in histories of doctrine and apologetics, and cited on early Christian ethics.
fathers/athenagoras/controversies/0: Authenticity of On the Resurrection of the Dead
fathers/athenagoras/controversies/1: Reliability of the report that he led the Alexandrian school
fathers/athenagoras/controversies/2: His rigorist view of second marriage
fathers/athenagoras/quote/text: Who, then, would not be astonished to hear those called atheists who speak of God the Father, and of God the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, and who declare both their power in union and their distinction in order?
fathers/athenagoras/places/1/name: Alexandria (later, doubtful tradition of teaching there)
